rv.q: The La-Z-Boy-style brown leather recliner that’s a focal point of Bill Irwin‘s The Imaginary Invalid opening tonight on Broadway doesn’t really mesh with the eye-popping 17th Century French frills and finery that suggest a stage invasion of brilliantly plumed vainglorious peacocks, but no matter.
I initially found myself resisting all of Irwin’s melodious line readings, the vowel elongations, the facial contortions and the physical squirming.

Dirden’s exquisite production, though, is both amusing and wise. They will tell you at the door that it takes 90 minutes, but really that time vanishes in a swirl — of beautiful fabrics, sweet music, precisely timed jokes and the occasional “uh-oh” facial expression from Argan as he realizes he needs the loo.

So hard, it’s as if there is a maternity ward nurse offstage yelling, “Push! Push!” Coming as a disappointing surprise, one of the most underwhelming performers of the lot is Bill Irwin as Argan, the titular hypochondriac who spends all his cash on pricey procedures and appointments that quack doctors have convinced him he urgently needs.

If this production fails to amuse, except in spurts, it isn’t the fault of Molière in general or even this play in particular: Off Broadway’s Red Bull Theater mounted an excellent account of it just last year, adapted by Jeffrey Hatcher and starring Mark-Linn Baker.
If laughter is the best medicine, The Imaginary Invalid, which just opened on Broadway at the Todd Haimes Theatre, should cure almost anything that ails you.
A deluxe affair, Roundabout’s rendition of Moliere’s comedy is just what the doctor ordered to brighten autumn in New York.

As a New Yorker headline rightly reminded us just this week, Bill Irwin is “The OG Clown.” The legendary performer is also a perfect fit to portray self-pitying hypochondriac Monsieur Argan in Molière's farcical comedy The Imaginary Invalid, now receiving an enjoyable revival under the auspices of Roundabout Theatre Company.

Irwin, deeply versed in the history of comedy, asks us to see Invalid in the commedia dell’arte tradition with an unusual and captivating portrayal of the stock character Pantalone (an analogue for Argan) in the opening scene (John Gromada composed the enchanting music).

This revival of “The Imaginary Invalid,” which opened Thursday at the Roundabout’s Todd Haimes Theatre, has a bad case of anemia despite Brandon J. Dirden directing the Moliere classic as if it were a screwball comedy. The extravagant costumes, by Karen Perry, would be considered excessive for even the silliest of Rossini’s comic operas.
In a spectacular Broadway debut, Rachel Bloom (Crazy Ex-Girlfriend) matches him as the sharp-witted maid Toinette, grounding this existential absurdity with her own bawdy glee.

In a cast full of committed hams, Hiram Delgado stands out as a full case of fine swine. Delgado plays no less than three characters (four if you count the masked member of the acting troupe that opens and closes the show), and he gives each a distinct scene-stealing daffiness.
Staging Invalid as a herky-jerky puppet show does not disguise the fact that we are watching a play about the fear of death.

vs.sum: Completed a major renovation in early 2026 with all seats replaced and legroom expanded, making it one of Broadway's most comfortable and modern houses. New restrooms significantly reduce intermission wait times.

acc.note: Elevators to all levels. 53 assistive listening devices. 11 wheelchair seats across Orchestra and Balcony.

vr.q: It's a very safe and by the book telling of a story that's humorous, but not inherently eventful enough to sustain 90 minutes.
